title: POC scoping - MedGlyph - data handling & benchmarks
summary: Initial POC scoping focused on data handling requirements for a healthcare-focused assistant. Discussed PII/redaction approach, logging and prompt storage options, retention windows, benchmarks (latency/p95, throughput), workload sizing, and a 4-week POC timeline. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share POC proposal and security docs; customer to provide example PII patterns and sample dataset for bench tests.
next_steps: Redwood to send POC proposal, pricing, and SOC2/ISO artifacts - Alex to send by 2025-02-15
Customer to share sample anonymized dataset and PII regex/rules - Maya to provide by 2025-02-18
Priya to run baseline bench on sample and share results - by 2025-02-21
Schedule technical deep dive for private deployment if required - tentatively 2025-02-25
action_items: Alex Chen - send security deck, SOC 2 report, and product brief - 2025-02-15
Maya Singh - provide sample PII patterns, retention policy, and regulatory constraints (HIPAA notes) - 2025-02-18
Priya Nair - run initial throughput/latency benchmark using provided sample (1k convs) and share raw results - 2025-02-21
Tom Fisher - confirm success criteria (latency p95, cost per 1k tokens, functional pass rate) - 2025-02-20
transcript:
[00:00:05] Alex Chen: Hey thanks everyone for joining, this is Alex from Redwood, I think we have Priya from our SE team on the call as well, hey priya.
[00:00:12] Priya Nair: hi all, yep hi.
[00:00:14] Dana Ruiz: Hi thanks, Dana here. We run ML at MedGlyph, and we want to scope a POC for an assistant that helps clinicians with chart summarization and triage, so obviously sensitive PII concerns.
[00:00:30] Tom Fisher: yep hi this is Tom product, and Maya from security will talk details on compliance.
[00:00:36] Maya Singh: hi all, thanks. My priority is understanding how Redwood will handle PII in logs, prompt retention, and what controls we can configure for retention and redaction.
[00:00:48] Alex Chen: great, that's exactly what we want to focus on. Quick agenda: success criteria and timelines, workload sizing (traffic & sizes), bench targets, and then deep into data handling: what gets logged, redaction options, retention windows, encryption/KMS, and prompt storage.
[00:01:05] Priya Nair: also will cover practical benching approach — what samples we need and what metrics we'll measure, e.g., p95 latency, throughput tokens/sec, and quality pass rate on a dev eval set.
[00:01:18] Dana Ruiz: for success criteria, we're thinking: 95% of inference calls under 500ms p95 for 512 token sequences, throughput to support 20 concurrent clinicians, and functional accuracy on our eval > 90% — is that reasonable?
[00:01:33] Priya Nair: that's reasonable for hosted high-performance models; the latency target depends on model choice and batching. For example if you want a smaller open model quantized it can meet <300ms for short sequences, for instruct tuned LLMs p95 in 400-700ms range is common.
[00:01:49] Tom Fisher: cost is also a factor, we have a target of under $0.05 per 1k tokens if possible, is that realistic?
[00:01:56] Alex Chen: costs vary a lot by model + deployment mode. Hosted with Redwood can be optimized — we also have Dedicated pools that change unit economics. We can scope a POC with two model variants: a cheaper quantized variant and a higher-quality variant. Bench will measure cost per effective request.
[00:02:13] Maya Singh: back to PII — do you persist prompts even for hosted mode? We need to know if prompts are stored, for how long, and how they are secured.
[00:02:22] Priya Nair: good question. Default behavior: request logs exist for debugging and observability; retention is configurable per account. For POC we can set retention to minimal — for example 7 days — or disable full prompt retention and keep only token-level metrics. We also support on-request redaction hooks before logs hit storage.
[00:02:39] Dana Ruiz: when you say redaction hooks, is that server-side library we drop into our app or something Redwood applies?
[00:02:45] Priya Nair: both patterns. We provide a client-side sanitizer library customers can run pre-request to strip/save PII, and we also offer server-side configurable redaction rules that run in the control plane before persisting. The server-side engine uses regex and ML-based detectors — note sometimes ML detectors have false positives/negatives, so we recommend client-side canonicalization + server-side guardrails.
[00:03:05] Maya Singh: and encryption? keys? where are logs stored? We need KMS integration and preferably bring-your-own-key.
[00:03:11] Alex Chen: we support customer-managed keys (BYOK) via KMS; logs are stored in encrypted object stores, and we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key rotation and access controls. For Private deployments you can keep logs behind your VPC and your own S3.
[00:03:26] Tom Fisher: good. For POC we'll probably start with hosted but need to know path to Dedicated/private if we decide to move. Timeline for that?
[00:03:33] Priya Nair: Dedicated typically takes longer due to capacity, but for POC we can simulate Dedicated characteristics — we can reserve a small dedicated pool or run workload in Hosted with strict routing to a pinned model. If you decide to go Private, typical lead time is several weeks for setup + networking.
[00:03:50] Dana Ruiz: ok, let's talk bench inputs. We'll provide 1,000 representative clinician prompts, average length ~400 tokens, with a tail of longer ones to 1,200 tokens. Peak concurrency expected 20 simultaneous sessions, average 3 requests/session per minute. Does that give you what you need?
[00:04:08] Priya Nair: yes that's really helpful. For benching we'll want a 1k sample and a 100-sample heavy tail to stress long-context. We'll measure p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, memory usage, and cost per 1k tokens. Also quality: we'll run your eval set to compute pass rate and key NLU metrics.
[00:04:28] Maya Singh: on prompt storage concerns — we are worried about prompts containing PHI being stored verbatim. Can you do selective prompt non-persistence?
[00:04:36] Priya Nair: yes we have options: 1) do not persist prompts at all (ephemeral logging) — loses debuggability; 2) persist only hashed prompts or token counts and metrics; 3) persist sanitized prompts after redaction rules. For POC we can enable sanitized persistence and also send you a copy of raw logs under secure transfer if needed.
[00:04:56] Alex Chen: just to add, function calling and tool outputs are treated similarly. We also have a policy engine where you can define retention windows (e.g., 7 days, 30 days, never) per route.
[00:05:07] Tom Fisher: one question — will you store user identifiers with requests? We want to avoid linking prompts to patient IDs in logs.
[00:05:13] Priya Nair: you can configure pseudonymous IDs in client so we never see direct patient IDs. On server side we can strip certain header fields before persisting.
[00:05:22] Dana Ruiz: regarding GDPR/HIPAA compliance, you mentioned SOC 2 earlier — we need HIPAA BAAs for production. Is that available?
[00:05:29] Alex Chen: Redwood currently has SOC 2 Type II; HIPAA BAA is available for Dedicated/Private customers — for Hosted we can discuss contractual BAAs. I'll send the security pack and SOC 2 artifacts.
[00:05:40] Maya Singh: please include details on audit logs, RBAC, SSO/SAML, and key rotation.
[00:05:44] Alex Chen: will do.
[00:05:48] [00:06:02] Priya Nair: shifting back to bench: success criteria concretely — p95 < 500ms for 512 tokens, throughput to sustain 20 concurrent clinicians with <5% queuing, and quality pass rate >= 90% on your eval. We'll instrument bench with realistic arrival patterns.
[00:06:18] Tom Fisher: what's the plan for model variants? We'll need to test two: a smaller quantized model for latency/cost, and a larger model for quality comparison.
[00:06:25] Priya Nair: yes we'll test both. We'll label them as Model-A (quantized) and Model-B (full-precision). We'll run A/B style bench, capture latency, throughput, and a quality sample. We'll produce a bench spreadsheet.
[00:06:36] Dana Ruiz: about prompt storage on your side — is there any chance prompts are used to further train models? We can't have that.
[00:06:43] Alex Chen: quick direct answer: Redwood does not use customer prompts to train public models. For hosted customers, data usage policies are explicit — we can guarantee non-training for your account and put that in contract. In Dedicated/Private, you control the data entirely.
[00:06:59] Maya Singh: good to have that in writing.
[00:07:02] [00:07:20] Tom Fisher: what about redaction granularity — can we remove specific entity types only and keep the rest? For example redact SSNs and patient names but keep procedure descriptions.
[00:07:29] Priya Nair: yes, rules are entity-based. You can define entity classes to redact. We support regex-based removal, token-level masking, or replacement with placeholders. We can also provide a redaction preview tool to run against your sample dataset.
[00:07:42] Dana Ruiz: what's the false positive rate for ML detectors? If names are replaced by initials frequently that might remove context.
[00:07:49] Priya Nair: ML detectors vary. Typical FP rates could be 2-8% depending on domain; we recommend running detectors on your sample and tuning rules. That's part of the POC.
[00:07:59] Maya Singh: retention windows: can different routes have different retention? For example, clinician-facing assistant retain 7 days, audit logs retained 365 days.
[00:08:08] Alex Chen: yes configurable per-route policies. Audit logs (access control and who viewed what) typically retained longer and are separate from request/response logs.
[00:08:16] [00:08:34] Priya Nair: a practical POC timeline we propose: Week 0: kickoff + data & security intake; Week 1: bench setup and initial runs on provided samples; Week 2: run expanded bench + quality eval + iterate redaction rules; Week 3: finalize bench, handoff report + recommendations. So a 3-4 week POC.
[00:08:51] Dana Ruiz: we have a compliance board meeting on 3/10, so if we can finish by then that'd be ideal. This timeline aligns.
[00:08:57] Tom Fisher: ok good. On monitoring: we'd like token-level cost breakdown per route. Is that available in the console?
[00:09:05] Alex Chen: yes Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns by route and model. You can also export raw telemetry to your SIEM.
[00:09:12] Maya Singh: export to our SIEM — fine, but ensure logs are redacted before export or we want an option for raw export to our secure bucket.
[00:09:19] Priya Nair: we support both: sanitized exports, or raw export to a customer-controlled S3 with encryption and access restrictions. For raw export we'd recommend Private or Dedicated.
[00:09:30] [00:09:46] Tom Fisher: for bench metrics, can you also include memory footprint and GPU utilization so we can estimate scaling/cost?
[00:09:52] Priya Nair: yes we'll capture GPU memory, utilization, average batch sizes, and latency by token length. We'll also capture KV cache hit rates if we're using long context caching.
[00:10:03] Dana Ruiz: what is KV cache? I've seen docs that say KV cache and sometimes people say K-V cash, lol.
[00:10:09] Priya Nair: ha, key-value cache — it's the internal cache of past key/values for auto-regressive decoding. It improves throughput for multi-turn by reusing past computation.
[00:10:17] Maya Singh: do you persist KV cache between requests? That seems risky.
[00:10:21] Priya Nair: KV cache is ephemeral and tied to inference instance — it is not persisted to long-term storage unless you explicitly configure session persistence. For POC we'll keep it ephemeral.
[00:10:31] [00:10:45] Alex Chen: quick note on fallback: Redwood supports routing to a lower-cost model if capacity is constrained; for critical flows you can configure fail-open or fail-closed policies. Important to decide for POC what your availability tradeoffs are.
[00:10:59] Tom Fisher: we probably want failover to the lower-cost model but with clear flag to degrade functionality rather than return an error.
[00:11:06] Priya Nair: got it — we'll show examples in the POC report.
[00:11:10] [00:11:27] Dana Ruiz: any limitations on redaction for structured fields like dates or microdata embedded in free text? Our notes often have embedded PHI in weird formats.
[00:11:36] Priya Nair: structured detection works better but free text edge cases are harder. For those we recommend two-layer approach: client canonicalization + server ML detectors + manual review for critical flows. You can also configure a human-in-the-loop redaction approval if needed.
[00:11:50] Maya Singh: human-in-the-loop seems heavy but could be used for flagged items. We'll monitor recall/precision during POC.
[00:11:59] [00:12:15] Tom Fisher: about metrics we want to see in the POC deliverable: bench spreadsheet, latency percentiles, cost per 1k tokens, GPU/mem utilization, redaction stats (FP, FN estimated), and a runbook for moving to Dedicated.
[00:12:28] Priya Nair: yep we'll include all that plus configuration snippets for redaction policies and example client-side sanitizer.
[00:12:36] Dana Ruiz: regarding prompt storage, would you consider encrypting prompts at rest with customer KMS and also storing them in a separate bucket?
[00:12:44] Alex Chen: yes, we can place logs into customer-controlled buckets and encrypt with customer KMS. That is typical for customers with strict data governance.
[00:12:52] Maya Singh: and access to those logs will be controlled by our IAM — we want minimal Redwood access.
[00:12:57] Priya Nair: we can restrict Redwood access for raw logs; for hosted we may need minimal support access under strict controls; for Dedicated/Private you control access fully.
[00:13:07] [00:13:25] Tom Fisher: is there any PII left in model-level telemetry like embeddings? If we store embeddings, is there a risk of reconstructing PHI?
[00:13:33] Priya Nair: embeddings can leak content; we recommend not storing raw embeddings for PHI content or to store them encrypted, and treat them under the same retention/redaction rules. For the POC we'll not persist any embeddings unless you ask and will show options.
[00:13:46] Dana Ruiz: good — please include that recommendation.
[00:13:50] Alex Chen: ok let's capture some concrete acceptance criteria for the POC so we can sign off at the end.
[00:13:55] Priya Nair: suggested acceptance criteria: 1) Bench meets p95 latency target for primary model or defined fallback performance thresholds; 2) Quality pass rate >= agreed threshold on eval set; 3) Redaction pipeline reduces raw PHI exposure to below agreed FP/FN levels or manual review thresholds; 4) Security artifacts provided and any contractual BAAs flagged for next phase.
[00:14:16] Tom Fisher: sounds good. We'll finalize thresholds in writing — for now we'll call p95 <500ms and quality >=90%.
[00:14:23] Maya Singh: and redaction FP <=5% and FN <=2% on the sample? We'll see.
[00:14:29] Priya Nair: we'll measure and iterate.
[00:14:33] [00:14:50] Dana Ruiz: any gotchas we should be aware of during benching?
[00:14:55] Priya Nair: watch out for sequence length distribution — longer tails increase latency and memory. Also batching strategy can increase throughput but adds some queuing delay. We'll simulate realistic arrival patterns rather than constant load.
[00:15:07] Tom Fisher: about batching — can we control max latency budget per route so batching won't violate p95?
[00:15:12] Priya Nair: yes you can set max batch latency thresholds; Redwood's runtime can do continuous batching subject to your latency SLOs. We'll show config examples.
[00:15:21] Alex Chen: also note that quantization choices affect top-k sampling determinism; if you need reproducible outputs we can pin seeds and model variants in the POC.
[00:15:33] [00:15:49] Maya Singh: any legal concerns about storing pseudonymous patient IDs? We need to check our counsel but generally we'd prefer not to store identifiers at all.
[00:15:57] Alex Chen: understood — recommend using ephemeral UUIDs and mapping on your side only.
[00:16:03] Priya Nair: ok next I'll outline the data artifacts we need from you: - anonymized sample dataset (1k requests) - PII rules / regex list - retention policy matrix - list of routes and expected traffic per route.
[00:16:18] Dana Ruiz: we'll provide that, though for legal reasons anonymized only.
[00:16:23] Tom Fisher: we'll also provide an eval set of 200 labeled cases for quality scoring.
[00:16:27] Priya Nair: perfect.
[00:16:30] [00:16:45] Alex Chen: on administrative side, I'll put together the POC SOW and send pricing for a 4-week engagement; that will include bench time, SE hours, and a security review.
[00:16:55] Maya Singh: pricing and SOW please, and include an option for Dedicated pilot pricing.
[00:16:59] Alex Chen: will do.
[00:17:03] Priya Nair: one more technical note: when we do redaction preview we'll provide a small report listing redacted spans and confidence scores so your team can tune rules.
[00:17:13] Dana Ruiz: that will be helpful.
[00:17:15] [00:17:32] Tom Fisher: about observability, we want alerting for redaction errors or sudden increase in PHI hits. Is that supported?
[00:17:40] Priya Nair: yes you can set alerts on metrics such as PHI-detection rate, redaction failures, error rates, latency SLO breaches. We'll wire alerts to PagerDuty or your Slack.
[00:17:51] Maya Singh: can alerts be routed to our security inbox only?
[00:17:54] Alex Chen: yes role-based alerting is possible.
[00:17:57] [00:18:10] Dana Ruiz: ok let's recap next steps.
[00:18:14] Alex Chen: recap: Redwood will send POC proposal, security pack (SOC2), sample config snippets, and a bench plan. Customer will share anonymized sample, PII rules, and retention needs. SE will run bench and share results in spreadsheet. We'll plan a technical deep-dive if Private/Dedicated is requested.
[00:18:33] Tom Fisher: agreed.
[00:18:36] Maya Singh: thanks, I'll follow up with the PII list.
[00:18:39] Dana Ruiz: thanks everyone.
[00:18:42] Alex Chen: thanks — we'll target sending docs tomorrow. bye.
[00:18:48] [END OF TRANSCRIPT]
